Effusion.definition: Pleural effusion is the accumulation of fluid in the pleural space around the lungs, which can compress lung tissue and impair breathing.
Effusion.causes: Common causes include infections (pneumonia, tuberculosis), heart failure, liver or kidney disease, and malignancy.
Effusion.symptoms: Shortness of breath, chest pain (especially on breathing), cough; severe cases cause significant breathing difficulty.
Effusion.severity: Ranges from mild to life-threatening depending on fluid volume and cause.
Effusion.risk: Higher risk when large volume, rapid accumulation, or associated with serious conditions (e.g., cancer, severe infection).
Effusion.diagnosis: Chest X-ray, ultrasound, CT scan; fluid analysis (thoracentesis) to determine cause.
Effusion.treatment: Treat underlying cause; medications; therapeutic drainage (thoracentesis); chest tube for large or recurrent effusions.
Effusion.reversibility: Often reversible if underlying cause is treated; may recur if cause persists.
Effusion.when_to_seek_help: Immediate care if severe breathlessness, chest pain, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Atelectasis.definition: Atelectasis is the partial or complete collapse of lung tissue, reducing gas exchange.
Atelectasis.causes: Airway obstruction (mucus plug), shallow breathing post-surgery, tumors, or external compression.
Atelectasis.symptoms: Shortness of breath, rapid breathing; mild cases may be asymptomatic.
Atelectasis.severity: Mild to severe depending on extent of lung involved.
Atelectasis.risk: Higher after surgery, prolonged bed rest, or with airway obstruction.
Atelectasis.diagnosis: Chest X-ray, CT scan; clinical examination.
Atelectasis.treatment: Deep breathing exercises, physiotherapy, bronchoscopy (if blockage), oxygen therapy.
Atelectasis.when_to_seek_help: Seek care if persistent breathlessness or after surgery with breathing difficulty.

Infiltration.definition: Pulmonary infiltration refers to substances (fluid, cells) filling lung tissue, often due to infection or inflammation.
Infiltration.causes: Commonly pneumonia, inflammatory conditions, or fluid overload.
Infiltration.severity: Variable; can be serious in widespread infection.
Infiltration.risk: Higher in elderly, immunocompromised, or untreated infections.
Infiltration.diagnosis: Chest X-ray/CT showing opacities; lab tests for infection.
Infiltration.treatment: Antibiotics (if bacterial), supportive care, treating underlying cause.
Infiltration.when_to_seek_help: Fever with breathlessness, worsening cough, or low oxygen symptoms.

Nodule.definition: A pulmonary nodule is a small, round growth in the lung, usually less than 3 cm.
Nodule.causes: Infections, benign growths, or early-stage tumors.
Nodule.severity: Usually low risk if small and stable; risk increases with size and growth.
Nodule.risk: Higher in smokers, older age, or growing nodules.
Nodule.diagnosis: CT scan; follow-up imaging; biopsy if suspicious.
Nodule.treatment: Observation for benign nodules; biopsy/surgery if malignant.
Nodule.reversibility: Benign nodules may remain stable; malignant ones require treatment.
Nodule.complications: Potential progression to cancer if malignant.
Nodule.when_to_seek_help: If nodule grows, symptoms appear, or doctor recommends further evaluation.

Pneumothorax.definition: Pneumothorax is the presence of air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse.
Pneumothorax.causes: Spontaneous rupture of lung blebs, trauma, or medical procedures.
Pneumothorax.symptoms: Sudden chest pain, shortness of breath.
Pneumothorax.severity: Can be life-threatening if large or tension pneumothorax.
Pneumothorax.risk: Higher in tall, thin individuals, smokers, or lung disease patients.
Pneumothorax.treatment: Observation (small cases), needle aspiration, chest tube insertion, surgery if recurrent.
Pneumothorax.reversibility: Often reversible with treatment; recurrence possible.
Pneumothorax.when_to_seek_help: Immediate emergency care for sudden chest pain and breathlessness.

Mass.definition: A lung mass is a larger abnormal growth (>3 cm) in the lung, potentially malignant.
Mass.symptoms: Persistent cough, chest pain, weight loss, coughing blood.
Mass.risk: Higher in smokers, older individuals, or family history of cancer.
Mass.treatment: Depends on cause: surgery, chemotherapy, radiation.
Mass.reversibility: Depends on diagnosis; benign masses may be managed, malignant require treatment.
Mass.when_to_seek_help: Immediate evaluation for persistent symptoms or suspicious imaging findings.
